payload.idea_summary: A space probe traveling at high speed between two stationary planets emits identical radio pulses forwards and backwards; the candidate must compare the speed, frequency, and wavelength of the pulses as received at each planet.

schema_invariant.core_move: Predict the observed frequency, wavelength, and speed of electromagnetic radiation by integrating the Doppler effect with the constancy of the speed of light in a vacuum.
what_must_not_change: The speed of the EM wave must remain constant (c) regardless of the source's motion.
The frequency and wavelength must shift according to the relative motion (approach = blueshift, recession = redshift).
The inverse relationship between observed frequency and wavelength.
what_can_change: The specific physical scenario (e.g., one source emitting in two directions instead of a single unidirectional source).
The objects involved (probe and planets instead of a star and Earth).
The format of the question (comparing two received signals rather than comparing a received signal to the emitted rest-frame signal).

discrimination_mechanism.reasoning_hinge: The candidate must decouple the wave speed from the source speed (resisting Galilean velocity addition) while still applying the source speed to the Doppler shift of frequency and wavelength.
discrimination_mechanism.why_top_students_win: They recognize that the speed of light in a vacuum is an invariant $c$ for all observers, but the relative approach/recession still alters the received frequency and wavelength.
discrimination_mechanism.why_mid_students_miss: They will either incorrectly apply Galilean velocity addition (claiming the forward pulse travels at $c+v$ and the backward at $c-v$), or they will over-apply the invariance of $c$ and assume that if speed doesn't change, neither do frequency and wavelength.

goldilocks_complexity_audit.main_physics_principle: Constancy of the speed of EM waves in a vacuum.
goldilocks_complexity_audit.supporting_idea_if_any: Qualitative Doppler effect (redshift/blueshift) for approaching and receding sources.

payload.reference_alignment: Maintains the exact conceptual difficulty of the reference by testing the same misconception traps (variable $c$ vs variable $f/\lambda$), but uses a symmetrical two-observer setup to make it feel fresh.
payload.visual_brief: No visual is needed. The text description of a probe between Planet X and Planet Y is sufficient and unambiguous.
payload.why_still_on_spec: The constancy of the speed of light in a vacuum and the qualitative nature of redshift/blueshift (Doppler effect for EM waves) are explicit standard requirements in GCSE and ESAT Physics.
constraints_used: no full equations unless the schema requires them

intended_wrong_paths.mistake: Applying Galilean velocity addition to light (forward speed = $c+v$, backward speed = $c-v$).
intended_wrong_paths.distractor_role: Options where the speeds of the two pulses are different.

intended_wrong_paths.mistake: Assuming that because the speed is constant, the frequency and wavelength must also be constant (no Doppler shift).
intended_wrong_paths.distractor_role: Option stating all properties are identical for both planets.

intended_wrong_paths.mistake: Inverting the Doppler shift (associating approach with redshift/lower frequency).
intended_wrong_paths.distractor_role: Option with correct constant speed but reversed inequalities for frequency and wavelength.

payload.difficulty_rationale: It requires zero calculation but strong conceptual clarity. The trap of adding source velocity to wave velocity is a classic, highly discriminating misconception that neatly separates rote memorizers from students with genuine physical intuition.

anti_plug_and_chug_check.why_not: There are no numbers to plug in; the question requires a conceptual comparison of variables across two different reference frames based on physical postulates.

mcq_viability.reason: The permutation of possible relationships (speed equal/unequal, frequency higher/lower, wavelength higher/lower) provides a clean set of distinct, plausible multiple-choice options.
